note: Shows accuracy collapsing on low-probability inputs even for deterministic tasks, which is a concrete reason an audit should test edge cases, not averages.
title: Embers of autoregression show how large language models are shaped by the problem they are trained to solve
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

reading.body:
Accuracy on deterministic tasks collapses when the input or answer is improbable, so model evaluation must test edge cases rather than averages.

The pattern is consistent across five models and eleven tasks. GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Claude 3, Llama 3, and Gemini 1.0 all lose accuracy as the task, the answer, or the input becomes less likely. The sharpest illustration is GPT-4 decoding a simple cipher: 51 percent correct when the output sentence was likely, 13 percent when it was unlikely, on a task with one right answer. The authors trace this to the training objective itself, guessing the next word in web text, which biases the model toward probable outputs regardless of what the task requires.

For AI systems generally, this is a reliability problem that scales with deployment. Rare inputs are exactly what production traffic contains, and a model that degrades on them fails precisely where it is hardest to notice. The practical consequence is that audits and pilots built on representative or average examples will overstate performance. Edge cases belong in the test set, not outside it.

What the data does not cover is the compute or power side of the story. Nothing here speaks to training scale, data center capacity, or grid constraints, and the paper's finding is about the training objective rather than the resources behind it. The result also does not establish how these failures compound in multi-step or agentic use, which the eleven tasks do not test.

explain_beginner: This paper asks why chatbots and similar AI systems sometimes fail in odd ways. The authors say these systems were trained mainly to guess the next word in internet text. That training pushes them toward likely words and sentences. The team tested five popular models on eleven tasks. They found that accuracy drops when the task, the answer, or the input is unlikely. In one example, GPT 4 decoded a simple cipher correctly 51 percent of the time for a likely sentence but only 13 percent for an unlikely one, even though the task has one correct answer. This matters because people should not trust these systems in unusual situations.
explain_business: This research suggests that AI language tools can become much less reliable when they face unusual requests, rare answers, or uncommon inputs. The authors tested five major models on eleven tasks and found this pattern repeatedly. In one test, GPT 4 solved a simple cipher far less often when the answer was an unlikely sentence, even though the task had a fixed correct answer. For business leaders, the practical lesson is to avoid relying on these tools for rare or edge case work without checks. It also means audits and pilots should include unusual examples, not just average performance, before deployment decisions.
explain_practitioner: The authors argue that because language models are trained to guess the next word in web text, their behavior reflects that goal. They predicted that three probability factors would affect accuracy: how common the task is, how common the desired answer is, and how common the given input is. They tested GPT 3.5, GPT 4, Claude 3, Llama 3, and Gemini 1.0 across eleven tasks. The results supported their predictions. A striking case involved GPT 4 decoding a simple cipher: accuracy was 51 percent when the output sentence was likely, but 13 percent when it was unlikely, despite the task being deterministic.
